3: Thus sometimes, to alleviate his pain, One of the sinners would display his back, And in less time conceal it than it lightens.
8: As on the brink of water in a ditch The frogs stand only with their muzzles out, So that they hide their feet and other bulk,
13: So upon every side the sinners stood; But ever as Barbariccia near them came, Thus underneath the boiling they withdrew.
17: I saw, and still my heart doth shudder at it, One waiting thus, even as it comes to pass One frog remains, and down another dives;
22: And Graffiacan, who most confronted him, Grappled him by his tresses smeared with pitch, And drew him up, so that he seemed an otter.
27: I knew, before, the names of all of them, So had I noted them when they were chosen, And when they called each other, listened how.
32: “O Rubicante, see that thou do lay Thy claws upon him, so that thou mayst flay him,” Cried all together the accursed ones.
37: And I: “My Master, see to it, if thou canst, That thou mayst know who is the luckless wight, Thus come into his adversaries’ hands.”
42: Near to the side of him my Leader drew, Asked of him whence he was; and he replied: “I in the kingdom of Navarre was born;
46: My mother placed me servant to a lord, For she had borne me to a ribald knave, Destroyer of himself and of his things.
50: Then I domestic was of good King Thibault; I set me there to practise barratry, For which I pay the reckoning in this heat.”
55: And Ciriatto, from whose mouth projected, On either side, a tusk, as in a boar, Caused him to feel how one of them could rip.
59: Among malicious cats the mouse had come; But Barbariccia clasped him in his arms, And said: “Stand ye aside, while I enfork him.”
63: And to my Master he turned round his head; “Ask him again,” he said, “if more thou wish To know from him, before some one destroy him.”
67: The Guide: “Now tell then of the other culprits; Knowest thou any one who is a Latian, Under the pitch?” And he: “I separated
71:
Lately from one who was a neighbour to it; Would that I still were covered up with him, For I should fear not either claw nor hook!”

And Libicocco: “We have borne too much;” And with his grapnel seized him by the arm, So that, by rending, he tore off a tendon.
75: Eke Draghignazzo wished to pounce upon him Down at the legs; whence their Decurion Turned round and round about with evil look.
79: When they again somewhat were pacified, Of him, who still was looking at his wound, Demanded my Conductor without stay:
82: “Who was that one, from whom a luckless parting Thou sayest thou hast made, to come ashore?” And he replied: “It was the Friar Gomita,
86:
He of Gallura, vessel of all fraud, Who had the enemies of his Lord in hand, And dealt so with them each exults thereat;

Money he took, and let them smoothly off, As he says; and in other offices A barrator was he, not mean but sovereign.
90:
Foregathers with him one Don Michael Zanche Of Logodoro; and of Sardinia To gossip never do their tongues feel tired.

O me! see that one, how he grinds his teeth; Still farther would I speak, but am afraid Lest he to scratch my itch be making ready.”
94: And the grand Provost, turned to Farfarello, Who rolled his eyes about as if to strike, Said: “Stand aside there, thou malicious bird.”
99: “If you desire either to see or hear,” The terror-stricken recommenced thereon, “Tuscans or Lombards, I will make them come.
103: But let the Malebranche cease a little, So that these may not their revenges fear, And I, down sitting in this very place,
107: For one that I am will make seven come, When I shall whistle, as our custom is To do whenever one of us comes out.”
110: Cagnazzo at these words his muzzle lifted, Shaking his head, and said: “Just hear the trick Which he has thought of, down to throw himself!”
114: Whence he, who snares in great abundance had, Responded: “I by far too cunning am, When I procure for mine a greater sadness.”
118: Alichin held not in, but running counter Unto the rest, said to him: “If thou dive, I will not follow thee upon the gallop,
122: But I will beat my wings above the pitch; The height be left, and be the bank a shield To see if thou alone dost countervail us.”
126: O thou who readest, thou shalt hear new sport! Each to the other side his eyes averted; He first, who most reluctant was to do it.
130: The Navarrese selected well his time; Planted his feet on land, and in a moment Leaped, and released himself from their design.
134: Whereat each one was suddenly stung with shame, But he most who was cause of the defeat; Therefore he moved, and cried: “Thou art o’ertakern.”
138: But little it availed, for wings could not Outstrip the fear; the other one went under, And, flying, upward he his breast directed;
142: Not otherwise the duck upon a sudden Dives under, when the falcon is approaching, And upward he returneth cross and weary.
146: Infuriate at the mockery, Calcabrina Flying behind him followed close, desirous The other should escape, to have a quarrel.
150: And when the barrator had disappeared, He turned his talons upon his companion, And grappled with him right above the moat.
155:
But sooth the other was a doughty sparhawk To clapperclaw him well; and both of them Fell in the middle of the boiling pond.

A sudden intercessor was the heat; But ne’ertheless of rising there was naught, To such degree they had their wings belimed.
156: Lamenting with the others, Barbariccia Made four of them fly to the other side With all their gaffs, and very speedily
157: This side and that they to their posts descended; They stretched their hooks towards the pitch-ensnared, Who were already baked within the crust,
158:
And in this manner busied did we leave them.

Inferno: Canto XXIII
159: Silent, alone, and without company We went, the one in front, the other after, As go the Minor Friars along their way.
161:
Upon the fable of Aesop was directed My thought, by reason of the present quarrel, Where he has spoken of the frog and mouse;

For ‘mo’ and ‘issa’ are not more alike Than this one is to that, if well we couple End and beginning with a steadfast mind.
163: And even as one thought from another springs, So afterward from that was born another, Which the first fear within me double made.
165: Thus did I ponder: “These on our account Are laughed to scorn, with injury and scoff So great, that much I think it must annoy them.
167:
If anger be engrafted on ill-will, They will come after us more merciless Than dog upon the leveret which he seizes,”

I felt my hair stand all on end already With terror, and stood backwardly intent, When said I: “Master, if thou hidest not
168:
Thyself and me forthwith, of Malebranche I am in dread; we have them now behind us; I so imagine them, I already feel them.”

And he: “If I were made of leaded glass, Thine outward image I should not attract Sooner to me than I imprint the inner.
170: Just now thy thoughts came in among my own, With similar attitude and similar face, So that of both one counsel sole I made.
